name: Meghanathaswamy Temple, Tirumeeyachur
deity: Shiva as Meghanathaswamy (Meganathar), with the goddess Lalithambikai
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by Tirugnanasambandar
period: Tevaram era; main shrine c. late 10th century
dynasty: Cholas (Sembiyan Mahadevi era; traditionally Kochengat Chola)
summary: Tirumeeyachur, near Peralam on the Kaveri, is revered above all for its goddess Lalithambikai and for the tradition that the Lalita Sahasranama — the thousand names of the Divine Mother — is bound to this shrine. Shiva is worshipped here as Meghanathaswamy, a Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by Tirugnana Sambandar, with the goddess at the devotional heart. Built as a raised Maadakovil with an elephant-backed vimana, the temple is a major centre of Devi worship in the delta.

sections.history: Tirumeeyachur is an ancient Shaiva centre near Peralam in the Tiruvarur country, on the banks of the Kaveri, revered in the seventh-century Tevaram by Sambandar. By tradition it is one of the raised Maadakovils ascribed to the early Chola king Kochengat Chola; scholars date the present main shrine to about the last quarter of the tenth century, in the time of the great Chola patron Sembiyan Mahadevi, whose era left fine sculpture at the temple. Its enduring fame, however, is as a seat of the goddess and of the Lalita Sahasranama.
sections.architecture: The temple is built as a Maadakovil on an elevated base, its vimana in the Gajaprishta form — curved like the back of an elephant. The sanctum enshrines Meghanathaswamy, but the devotional focus is the shrine of the goddess Lalithambikai, which holds a celebrated Chola-period panel of Shiva appeasing Parvati (Gangadhara). The complex also contains the separate Paadal Petra shrine of Sakalabhuvaneswarar, the Ilankoil, in its northern prakara.
sections.legends: The temple's great tradition is the Lalita Sahasranama, the thousand names of the Divine Mother. In the much-told account, when Parvati was displeased, the ashta vachinees — eight personifications of speech — soothed her by reciting her thousand names, and from this arose the Sahasranama; the sages Agastya and Hayagriva are also said to have received the hymn in connection with this shrine. Other traditions make Tirumeeyachur the birthplace of Garuda, tell of Yama worshipping here for longevity, and of Indra regaining his lost powers before the lord and the goddess.
sections.festivals: Festivals centred on the goddess are the heart of the calendar, with Navaratri and the Tamil month of Aadi drawing large gatherings of Devi devotees, and recitations of the Lalita Sahasranama especially cherished here. The Shaiva observances of Maha Shivaratri and Pradosham are also kept at the Meghanathaswamy sanctum, and the goddess's Fridays are particularly busy.
sections.experience: For devotees of the Divine Mother, Tirumeeyachur is a place of special pull, tied as it is to the Lalita Sahasranama. Pilgrims come above all for the darshan of Lalithambikai, chanting her thousand names, and the elevated Maadakovil, the elephant-backed vimana and the fine Chola sculpture reward the eye as the goddess rewards the heart.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tirumeeyachur is about 2 km from Peralam and near Nannilam in Tiruvarur district, roughly 15 km from Mayiladuthurai; the nearest rail heads are Peralam and Mayiladuthurai, with local buses and taxis to the village.
